title: Blooms Seen on Arrival
statement:
A garden has flowers. Flower i is in bloom from day flowers[i][0] to day flowers[i][1], both days included.

Visitor j comes on day visits[j]. Return an array whose j-th value is the number of flowers in bloom on the day visitor j comes. Keep the visitors in the order given.

examples.why: Day 4 is the last day of [1, 4], so that flower still counts. On day 5 it is gone, and [5, 5] blooms for its one day.
A one-day bloom counts only on exactly that day.
Identical flowers count separately, and two visitors may come on the same day.

hints: For one visitor on day t, a flower counts if it has started and has not ended yet. Can you count those two groups separately?
Flowers in bloom on day t = (flowers with start ≤ t) − (flowers with end < t). Every flower that ended before t also started before t, so the subtraction is exact.
Sort all starts and all ends once. Each count is then a binary search: upper bound of t in the starts, lower bound of t in the ends.

explain.intuition:
Checking every flower for every visitor is n · m work. Instead, split the question in two. The flowers blooming on day t are those that have started by day t, minus those that have already finished before day t. A flower that finished before t must also have started before t, so it sits in the first group and the subtraction removes it cleanly.

Both groups are "how many values in a sorted list are ≤ x" questions, so sort the starts and the ends separately and answer each visitor with two binary searches. It does not matter that the sorting separates each start from its end. This is the same counting a timeline UI does to show how many events are active at a cursor position.
steps: Collect all starts into one array and all ends into another; sort both.
For each visitor day t: started = number of starts ≤ t (upper bound).
ended = number of ends < t (lower bound), because a flower whose last day is t still counts.
The answer for the visitor is started − ended. Fill the result in the original visitor order.
pitfalls: Using ends ≤ t. That drops flowers on their last day; the first example gives 2 instead of 3 for day 4.
Sorting the visits and forgetting to put answers back in the original order.
Keeping starts and ends paired when sorting. Pairing is not needed and makes the counting harder.

solutions.title: Check every flower for every visitor
solutions.idea: For each visitor, count the flowers whose range contains the visit day.

solutions.title: Sorted starts and ends, binary search
solutions.idea: Blooming on day t = starts ≤ t minus ends < t. Two sorted arrays answer both counts by binary search.

solutions.title: Sweep visitors in day order
solutions.idea: Sort visitor indices by day and advance two pointers over the sorted starts and ends, so each pointer moves forward only once.
solutions.time: O(n log n + m log m)

followups: Flowers are added while visitors keep arriving (online). Which structure replaces the sorted arrays?
Return the busiest day in the garden instead, the day with the most flowers in bloom.
